title: Monitoring Models in Production — Data Drift and Concept Drift

questions.question: A model service answers every request with HTTP 200 and normal latency. What can it still hide?
options: Nothing, because a healthy service always returns correct predictions
Memory leaks, because HTTP 200 responses never allocate new memory
Wrong predictions, because the data moved away from the training data
Slow queries, because an HTTP 200 status means the request took over one second
questions.explanation: System health checks show that the service answers. They say nothing about whether the answers are still right for today's data.

questions.question: Fraudsters change tactics, so the same payment features now carry a different fraud risk. Which kind of drift is this?
options: Covariate drift, because P(x) changed
Prior drift, because P(y) changed alone
No drift, because the inputs look the same
Concept drift, because P(y | x) changed
questions.explanation: The input distribution can stay the same while the correct answer for each input changes. That is concept drift, and only labeled outcomes reveal it.

questions.question: One of 10 reference-decile bins holds 10 percent of the reference and 30 percent of the current window. What does this bin add to PSI?
options: About 1.10, the natural log of the ratio 0.30 / 0.10
About 0.66, three times the difference in shares
About 0.22, which is (0.30 - 0.10) times ln(3)
About 0.20, the difference between the two shares
questions.explanation: Each bin adds (current share minus reference share) times the log of their ratio. Here that is 0.20 times 1.099, about 0.22.

questions.question: A drift monitor checks 50 features every hour at alpha 0.05, and nothing has changed. About how many false alarms does it raise per day?
options: About 2.5
About 60
About 1200
None, because alpha protects every test
questions.explanation: The monitor runs 50 times 24, or 1200 tests per day. Each one has a 5 percent false-alarm rate, so about 60 fire on unchanged data.

questions.question: With one million events in each window, the KS test reports p = 2e-7 for a feature, and D is 0.004. What should the alert policy do?
options: Log it at most as a warning, because the effect size D is tiny
Page the on-call engineer, because the p-value is far below alpha
Retrain at once, because any significant result means concept drift
Ignore KS and switch to PSI, because KS is invalid for large windows
questions.explanation: Large samples make tiny gaps significant. The policy needs an effect-size threshold on D as well as a p-value threshold before it alerts a person.

questions.question: Input monitors stay quiet, but accuracy on newly labeled events falls from 0.95 to 0.78. What is the right next step?
options: Ignore it, because input drift tests found nothing wrong at all
Lower the PSI thresholds until the input monitors fire too
Retrain on the original training data with more epochs
Treat it as concept drift and collect recent labels to retrain
questions.explanation: Stable inputs with falling accuracy point to a change in P(y | x). Retraining on old labels teaches the old concept again, so recent labels come first.
